To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
EGTA stimulates inward INaCa by reducing submembrane calcium and inhibits outward INaCa by depleting cytoplasmic calcium.
EGTA stimulates INaCa by buffering submembrane calcium, that the apparent Ki for EGTa is 0.2-0.3 mM, and that EGTA inhibition of the outward INCa is due to calcium depletion.

EGTA (1) inhibits the inward INaCA current by depleting submembrane Ca2+ concentrations, (2) enhances the outward INaCA current at low EGTA concentration by increasing submembrane Ca concentrations, and (3) inhibits the outward INaC current at high EGTA concentrations by binding Ca2+ at the regulatory site of the exchanger.
In summary, our research is concerned with
calcium binding and release by the sodium-calcium exchanger in giant cardiac membrane vesicles.
calcium buffering by EGTP in giant cardiac membrane
the regulation of the Na+,Ca2+, exchanger in heart by intracellular calcium and by calcium buffers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EGTA acts as a simple calcium chelator and has no direct effect on INaCa.
the effect of EGTA on the exchanger current is due to the effect of EGTa on the free calcium concentration.
EGTA is not a specific inhibitor of the sodium-calcium exchanger.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the exchanger is regulated by submembrane calcium concentrations, and that calcium buffering can either inhibit or enhance exchanger activity depending on the direction of INaCa and the submembrane calcium concentration.
the exchanger is activated by calcium accumulation at the cytoplasmic membrane surface, but the rate and magnitude of activation is modulated by the rate of calcium entry into the cytoplasm.
the exchanger is regulated by calcium at both submembrane and regulatory sites, and that the calcium buffer, EGTA, can affect the exchanger by modulating the calcium at both of these sites.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the exchanger can operate at low cytoplasmic calcium concentrations (e.g. 0.1-1.0 microM) in the presence of EGTA (1-10 mM), and that the exchanger may be activated in the presence of low cytoplasm Ca2+ by a mechanism that involves calcium accumulation in the submembrane space.
EGTA is an effective calcium buffer for the study of INaCa in cardiac membranes.
INaCa is not regulated by calcium buffering.
